Start at https://www.google.com and complete the following task.

I’m in the UK and trying to work out whether starting a side hustle on top of my £55,500 salary is going to create extra tax admin, so could you check a few things in the browser for me? First, go to the official HMRC side-hustle guidance on taxhelpforhustlers.campaign.gov.uk and pull out the kinds of side-hustle income they say need to be reported, especially so I can tell whether things like reselling items online or doing delivery or other gig work would fall into those categories; please open the actual HMRC guidance page and leave it open so I can look at the wording myself. Then go to the Reed UK tax calculator on reed.co.uk, enter an annual salary of £55,500, and tell me the annual income tax figure it shows as my baseline; if the results page is separate, leave that open too so I can compare it with the HMRC guidance. After that, use Google to find a UK paycheck or salary calculator that shows a single pay-period net pay amount for a £55,500 salary, open the calculator result you use in its own tab, and report one estimated take-home amount for a single pay period. In the end, give me a short summary with the HMRC reportable income categories, the Reed annual income tax amount, the single-period net pay estimate, and a quick conclusion saying whether a side hustle in one of those HMRC categories would likely need reporting in addition to my salary.

Rules:

Hobby or hustle?

Understanding the tax rules for side hustles

Watch this page in British Sign Language (BSL)

Do you earn money from a hobby or other work outside your main job? Whether it’s casual earnings or a regular second income, there are tax rules that everyone must follow. From online selling and tutoring to delivery work and dog walking, here’s what you need to know. 

Made more than £1,000 from your side hustles?

Then it’s grown bigger than a hobby. Whether you get cash in hand or money paid straight to your bank account, you’ll need to tell HMRC so you can avoid any tax surprises. 

Check on GOV.UK to find out what to do
We’re talking about total income from all your side hustles between 6 April 2025 and 5 April 2026. 

If you’re just selling unwanted personal belongings from time to time, you probably don’t need to tell HMRC but it’s a good idea to check to make sure.

Why it’s important to follow the tax rules for side hustles 

It’s your responsibility to tell HMRC about your extra income when you need to. If not, there are consequences such as unexpected tax bills and penalties.

**Analyzing Available Resources**

I've been examining resources, specifically focusing on "taxhelpforhustles.campaign.gov.uk". So far, I've identified two key pages. The first covers tax rules for selling items, both handmade and bought, especially online. The second addresses tax for delivery drivers.


**Investigating Tax Guidance**

I'm now diving deeper into the HMRC guidance pages. I'm focusing on the main page questions, expanding the accordions to understand them. I'm also examining the subpages on selling items, and delivery driving tax rules. I will keep the HMRC guidance tab open for direct reference, as requested. I'm taking notes on reportable income, the £1,000 threshold, reselling, and delivery driving.

=== RESELLING / SELLING THINGS ===
Tax rules for selling things What you need to know to get your tax right Watch this page in British Sign Language (BSL) Is it a hobby or hustle? It’s important to understand when you need to tell HMRC about things you’ve sold, even if you think of it as just a hobby. This includes making sure you follow online selling tax rules. Just selling unwanted personal belongings from time to time? You don’t usually need to tell us. Selling things you’ve made or bought? For example, arts and crafts, food and drink, beauty and health products, digital creative products, or upcycled furniture – including through online marketplaces, auction sites, and selling platforms. Check on GOV.UK to find out what to do Earned more than £1,000 on top of your main job in the last tax year? If it’s from making or buying things to sell for a profit, as well as any other side hustles, you’ll need to tell us. The tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April. This is the amount you earn before factoring in expenses. It is not the same as profit. You may have to pay tax on money you made from side hustles if your total income, including your main job, was above the basic personal allowance of £12,570. Made £1,000 or less? You don’t need to let us know about that. How to tell HMRC if you need to Firstly, you should check if you need to tell HMRC about additional income . If you do need to tell us about extra income you’ve made from side hustles, you will need to register for Self Assessment as a sole trader. That’s because HMRC likely classes your side hustles as “trading” – as you receive income from selling goods or services. You will need to do this by 5 October. If you don’t tell HMRC when you need to, you could end up with an unexpected tax bill or penalty. Some examples of selling You buy items from car boot sales or charity shops with the intention to sell them for more money than you paid for them. This is something you do regularly. You need to tell HMRC about this money.  You upcycle second-hand pieces of furniture as a hobby with the intention to sell them. You made more than £1,000 selling them through local markets and online platforms between 6 April 2025 and 5 April 2026. You need to tell HMRC about this money. You make greetings cards which you sell online. You made over £1,000 selling the cards, so you need to tell HMRC. You buy wholesale bundles of vintage clothing which you then resell individually through onlin

=== SERVICES / GIG WORK ===
Tax advice for service providers From deliveries to dog walking, learn the tax rules for service hustles Watch this page in British Sign Language (BSL) This guide will help you understand when to tell HMRC about providing services on the side, even if you just think of it as a hobby. This includes the tax rules for delivery driving, tutoring, dog walking, gardening and more. Made more than £1,000 in the last tax year? Here is the breakdown of the checks and calculations you requested:

---

### 1. Open Tabs Reference
- **Tab ID 480038462**: HMRC Side-Hustle Campaign Guidance — *Tax Help for Hustles* (`https://taxhelpforhustles.campaign.gov.uk/`)  
  *(Note: The URL `taxhelpforhustlers.campaign.gov.uk` redirects to a GOV.UK 404 page; the official live campaign guidance is located at `taxhelpforhustles.campaign.gov.uk`)*
- **Tab ID 480038463**: Reed UK Tax Calculator Results for £55,500 salary (`https://www.reed.co.uk/tax-calculator/55500-annually`)
- **Tab ID 480038464**: MoneySavingExpert Income Tax Calculator Results for £55,500 salary (`https://www.moneysavingexpert.com/tax-calculator/`)
- **Tab ID 480038377**: Google Search (`https://www.google.com/search?q=UK+paycheck+salary+calculator+take+home+pay`)

---

### 2. HMRC Reportable Side-Hustle Income Categories
According to HMRC’s official guidance on *Tax Help for Hustles*, reportable side-hustle earnings fall into three main trading categories:

1. **Selling things (Making or Buying to Sell)**:
   - **Reselling online or offline**: Buying items (e.g., from charity shops, car boot sales, or wholesale lots) with the intention of selling them for a profit via platforms like eBay, Vinted, Etsy, or local markets.
   - **Making goods to sell**: Handcrafted items, art, food/drink, beauty products, digital goods, or upcycled furniture.
   - *Key distinction*: Occasionally selling off unwanted personal belongings does not usually need to be reported, but buying or making items to turn a profit is classed as trading.
2. **Providing services (Gig & Freelance Work)**:
   - Delivering food or parcels (e.g., Deliveroo, Uber Eats, Amazon Flex).
   - Ridesharing or taxi driving.
   - Dog walking, pet sitting, babysitting, cleaning, gardening, tutoring, and trades/repairs.
   - Hiring out equipment or renting out a personal parking space or garage.
   - *Note on apps*: HMRC explicitly states the same rules apply whether you find clients through digital platforms/apps or word of mouth.
3. **Creating content**:
   - Social media posts, online videos, podcasts, sponsored posts, and brand partnerships (including the monetary value of gifted products or perks).

**The £1,000 Trading Allowance Rule**:
- You must tell HMRC if your total **gross income** (total revenue before deducting expenses, not net profit) from all your side hustles combined exceeds **£1,000** in a tax year (6 April to 5 April).
- If your gross side-hustle income is £1,000 or less, you do not need to report it or pay tax on it.

---

### 3. Reed UK Tax Calculator Baseline (£55,500 Salary)
Entering £55,500 into the Reed UK Tax Calculator produces the following baseline annual deductions (standard tax code):
- **Annual Income Tax**: **£9,632.00**
- **Annual National Insurance**: £3,120.60
- **Annual Take-Home Pay**: £42,747.40

---

### 4. Single Pay-Period Net Pay Estimate (from Google Search)
Using the MoneySavingExpert Income Tax Calculator (found via Google search; *The Salary Calculator* was also checked from Google results but encountered a connection error `ERR_SOCKS_CONNECTION_FAILED`):
- **Estimated Net Take-Home Pay per Single Pay Period**:
  - **Monthly**: **£3,562.00** *(or £3,562.28 exact on Reed)*
  - **Weekly**: **£822.00** *(or £822.07 exact on Reed)*

---

### 5. Conclusion: Will Your Side Hustle Need Reporting?
- **Yes, if your gross earnings exceed £1,000**: Both online reselling (for profit) and gig work (such as deliveries or tutoring) are classed as trading activities by HMRC. 
- Because your £55,500 salary already uses up your entire £12,570 tax-free Personal Allowance and places you into the **40% higher-rate tax bracket** (which starts at £50,270), any side-hustle profit above the £1,000 trading allowance will be taxable at your 40% marginal rate.
- If your total side-hustle gross income exceeds £1,000 in the tax year, it will not be automatically sorted through your main job’s PAYE; you will need to register with HMRC for Self Assessment as a sole trader by 5 October following the end of the tax year and file a tax return. If gross income remains under £1,000, no reporting is required.

Hobby or hustle?

Understanding the tax rules for side hustles

Do you earn money from a hobby or other work outside your main job? Whether it’s casual earnings or a regular second income, there are tax rules that everyone must follow. From online selling and tutoring to delivery work and dog walking, here’s what you need to know. 

Made more than £1,000 from your side hustles?

Then it’s grown bigger than a hobby. Whether you get cash in hand or money paid straight to your bank account, you’ll need to tell HMRC so you can avoid any tax surprises. 

Check on GOV.UK to find out what to do

=== RESELLING / SELLING THINGS ===
Tax rules for selling things What you need to know to get your tax right Watch this page in British Sign Language (BSL) Is it a hobby or hustle? It’s important to understand when you need to tell HMRC about things you’ve sold, even if you think of it as just a hobby. This includes making sure you follow online selling tax rules. Just selling unwanted personal belongings from time to time? You don’t usually need to tell us. Selling things you’ve made or bought? For example, arts and crafts, food and drink, beauty and health products, digital creative products, or upcycled furniture – including through online marketplaces, auction sites, and selling platforms. Check on GOV.UK to find out what to do Earned more than £1,000 on top of your main job in the last tax year? If it’s from making or buying things to sell for a profit, as well as any other side hustles, you’ll need to tell us. The tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April. This is the amount you earn before factoring in expenses. It is not the same as profit. ### 2. HMRC Reportable Side-Hustle Income Categories
According to HMRC’s official guidance on *Tax Help for Hustles*, reportable side-hustle earnings fall into three main trading categories:

1. **Selling things (Making or Buying to Sell)**:
   - **Reselling online or offline**: Buying items (e.g., from charity shops, car boot sales, or wholesale lots) with the intention of selling them for a profit via platforms like eBay, Vinted, Etsy, or local markets.
   - **Making goods to sell**: Handcrafted items, art, food/drink, beauty products, digital goods, or upcycled furniture.
   - *Key distinction*: Occasionally selling off unwanted personal belongings does not usually need to be reported, but buying or making items to turn a profit is classed as trading.
2. **Providing services (Gig & Freelance Work)**:
   - Delivering food or parcels (e.g., Deliveroo, Uber Eats, Amazon Flex).
   - Ridesharing or taxi driving.
   - Dog walking, pet sitting, babysitting, cleaning, gardening, tutoring, and trades/repairs.
   - Hiring out equipment or renting out a personal parking space or garage.
   - *Note on apps*: HMRC explicitly states the same rules apply whether you find clients through digital platforms/apps or word of mouth.
3. **Creating content**:
   - Social media posts, online videos, podcasts, sponsored posts, and brand partnerships (including the monetary value of gifted products or perks).

**The £1,000 Trading Allowance Rule**:
- You must tell HMRC if your total **gross income** (total revenue before deducting expenses, not net profit) from all your side hustles combined exceeds **£1,000** in a tax year (6 April to 5 April).
- If your gross side-hustle income is £1,000 or less, you do not need to report it or pay tax on it.

### 5. Conclusion: Will Your Side Hustle Need Reporting?
- **Yes, if your gross earnings exceed £1,000**: Both online reselling (for profit) and gig work (such as deliveries or tutoring) are classed as trading activities by HMRC. 
- Because your £55,500 salary already uses up your entire £12,570 tax-free Personal Allowance and places you into the **40% higher-rate tax bracket** (which starts at £50,270), any side-hustle profit above the £1,000 trading allowance will be taxable at your 40% marginal rate.
- If your total side-hustle gross income exceeds £1,000 in the tax year, it will not be automatically sorted through your main job’s PAYE; you will need to register with HMRC for Self Assessment as a sole trader by 5 October following the end of the tax year and file a tax return. If gross income remains under £1,000, no reporting is required.
